groups.title: How the Internet Works
groups.question: Walk through what happens on the network when a client calls https://api.example.com/books, before your code even runs.

followUps.TCP/IP & the Packet Model: What does the TCP three-way handshake set up, and why does it matter for connection timeouts?
followUps.DNS — Domain Resolution & TTL: You move your API to a new IP, but some users still hit the old one. What is DNS TTL doing here?

evidence.text: A connection is set up before any data is sent: the two sides exchange a few messages (the handshake) and agree on starting sequence numbers.
TCP delivers bytes reliably and in order: lost packets are re-sent and reassembled in the right order.
Setting up the connection costs a round trip, which is why slow or unreachable servers show up as connect timeouts and why reusing connections (keep-alive) helps.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (TCP, IP, the handshake, SYN/ACK) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says TCP sends packets with no connection and no delivery guarantee.

evidence.text: The hostname is first turned into an IP address by asking DNS resolvers before the connection is made.
DNS answers are cached by resolvers and clients for the record's TTL.
Until the TTL runs out, clients keep using the cached old IP, so a moved server is still hit at its old address.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (DNS, TTL, resolver) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Describes TTL as response time or network latency.

groups.title: HTTP Fundamentals
groups.question: Explain how an HTTP request and response are built, and what HTTPS adds on top.

followUps.HTTP Methods, Headers & Status Codes: Why is using GET for an action that changes data a problem for caches and retries?
followUps.HTTPS & TLS Handshake: What two things does TLS give you, and what does the handshake cost in latency?

evidence.text: A request has a method, a path, headers and an optional body; a response has a status code, headers and a body.
Read methods like GET must not change data, because caches, proxies, crawlers or clients may store, repeat or retry them.
The status code tells the client what happened (success, client error, server error), so a failure must not be returned as 200.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (GET, POST, headers, status codes) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says GET and POST are interchangeable, or that the only difference is where parameters are visible.

evidence.text: TLS encrypts the traffic so others on the network can't read or alter it.
The server proves its identity with a certificate signed by an authority the client trusts.
The handshake adds round trips before the first request; reusing connections or session resumption reduces that cost.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (HTTPS, TLS, certificate, secure) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the certificate itself encrypts the data, or that TLS adds no latency.

groups.title: REST Architecture
groups.question: Explain what makes an API RESTful, and how you would test one without writing a frontend.

followUps.REST Constraints & Statelessness: Why does keeping session state on one server break scaling behind a load balancer?
followUps.API Clients — curl, Postman & Insomnia: How would you send a POST with a JSON body and an auth header from the terminal?

evidence.text: Each request carries everything the server needs (such as the auth token), so the server keeps no session between requests.
Because no single server holds a client's session, any instance behind a load balancer can serve any request, so servers can be added or removed freely.
Resources are identified by URLs and handled with standard HTTP methods.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (REST, stateless, resources) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says stateless means the API stores no data at all, for example no database.

evidence.text: Requests can be sent straight from the terminal or a tool like curl or Postman, without writing a frontend.
You set the method, headers (such as Content-Type and Authorization) and a JSON body yourself.
You see the raw status, headers and body, so you can tell whether a bug is in the client or the server.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (curl, Postman, Insomnia) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says curl can only send GET requests.

groups.title: Developer Tooling Baseline
groups.question: An API call from the browser returns the wrong data. Explain how you would inspect what was really sent and received.

followUps.Browser DevTools — Network Tab: What can the Network tab show you about a request that console.log can't?
followUps.HTTP Caching Basics — Cache-Control & ET: How do Cache-Control and ETags stop a client from downloading the same response again?

evidence.text: The Network tab shows the request exactly as the browser sent it: URL, method, headers and payload.
It shows what came back: status code, response headers, body and timing.
It shows things code logging can't, such as headers the browser added, preflight/CORS requests, cached responses and timing.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (DevTools, Network tab) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the Network tab shows what happened inside the server's code.

evidence.text: Cache-Control tells the client or CDN how long it may reuse a stored response without asking the server again.
With an ETag the client sends it back (If-None-Match); if nothing changed the server answers 304 with no body, so nothing is downloaded again.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Cache-Control, ETag) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says no-cache means the response is never stored.
